title: The Monty Hall problem: why switching doors doubles your chances
description: Three doors, one car, two goats. You pick a door; the host opens a different door to reveal a goat — and offers you the chance to switch. Your instincts say it makes no difference. Your instincts are wrong.

body.heading: The set-up
paragraphs: The puzzle is named after Monty Hall, host of the television show Let's Make a Deal. Behind one of three doors is a car; behind the other two, goats. You choose door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens door 3 to reveal a goat, and asks: do you want to switch to door 2?

Most people feel the remaining doors are a coin flip — fifty-fifty. In 1990, columnist Marilyn vos Savant answered “switch” in her magazine column and received thousands of angry letters, including some from mathematicians. She was right.

body.heading: Why switching wins
paragraphs: Your first pick had a 1-in-3 chance of being the car — and a 2-in-3 chance of being a goat. The host's reveal does not change your door's odds; it concentrates all of that 2-in-3 chance onto the one unopened door, because the host can never open the car door by accident.

Say it plainly: if your first pick was a goat (which happens two times out of three), the host is forced to leave the car as the only other closed door — so switching wins. Only when your first pick was already the car (one time in three) does switching lose.

body.heading: Try it: play fifty rounds
paragraphs: Do not argue — experiment. Use three cups and a coin, with one player as host who always reveals a goat after the guess. Play 25 rounds always staying and 25 always switching, and tally the wins. The switch column should pull ahead convincingly.
Then scale the intuition: imagine 100 doors, you pick one, and the host opens 98 goat doors. Would you switch then? Almost everyone would — and it is the same decision, wearing a bigger coat.

takeaway: The Monty Hall problem is a trap for intuition: the host's knowledge changes the odds, and switching quietly doubles your chance of the car.
